I’m worried that in a building of 60 flats, people won’t vote honestly if they think Bích can see who voted against her. Ade’s team is asking me to go door-to-door to collect paper votes instead, but our bylaws don’t actually authorize a parallel ballot. I’ve got 48 hours before voting closes. What should I do?

I’m a class parent for my son’s eighth-grade trip to Washington, D.C., and I just found out the fundraising count Jenna gave the principal’s office last Wednesday is off by about $1,700—some donations got double-counted, and a couple of pledges from the fall never came through. The principal, Dr. Okonkwo, is relying on those numbers to finalize the bus contract by next Tuesday, and if we lose the deposit slot, 47 kids lose the trip. Jenna is already overwhelmed—her mother’s been in hospice since February—and I know she didn’t mean any harm, but if I flag the error officially, Dr. Okonkwo will have to open a review, and that could fall hard on her. If I quietly scramble the missing money through our parent network, I might cover the gap without anyone getting hurt, but it means deliberately working around the reporting process the school passed in the spring. Ravi on the PTA keeps telling me the only sacred thing here is getting those kids to the Lincoln Memorial—everything else is just paperwork. How do I hold this?

Pastor Jeffries asked to meet tomorrow morning. I’m almost certain he’s going to push for my blessing on the new youth-disciple streaming contract—twelve-year-olds signing exclusive online mentorship rights to one church network, and parents only get aggregated “spiritual progress” dashboards, not the actual recordings. He keeps framing it as the only way to protect kids from secular influencers: “What if one lost soul becomes the next streaming predator? Isn’t one eternal childhood worth full visibility?” The board already voted, but my signature as youth ministry director is the last barrier. If I refuse, they’ll frame me as soft on child safety and I’ll lose the funding for the summer retreat where Chidi and Svetlana finally started opening up about their doubts. I can’t see a third option that keeps both the retreat and the kids off a permanent digital leash. What do I do?

prompt:
Coach,

We just got the official roster for the U20 national camp. My brother Ahmet made the 28—bare minimum, but he’s in. The problem is I’m one of the four selectors who’ll cut it to 22 next week, and I’ve just seen the medical report everyone else will receive tomorrow morning. Ahmet’s been hiding a stress reaction in his fibula. It’s not a fracture yet, but it’s the kind of thing that goes if you crush him with two-a-days in a camp at altitude, and you ruin him for the club season. The other three selectors want to keep him—his 1500m time puts him inside the top eight on paper, and this camp is the only qualifier pathway left. Our father was a flag-bearer for this program in ‘92, so my staying silent would look like family loyalty. But I know the full picture and they don’t. I need to know how to handle Thursday’s selection meeting without wrecking the group’s trust or my brother’s future. What would you do?

My brother Lars is running for township supervisor here in Oakridge. It’s been ugly. Yesterday a neighbor handed me a thumb drive with four years of the current supervisor’s private emails—Nomvula from his office apparently pulled them off a shared machine without anyone knowing. The neighbor said, “You didn’t get this from me, but if these hit the local paper three days before the election, Lars wins.” I skimmed enough to see the supervisor took a golf trip on a developer’s dime and lied about the ethics filing. Part of me wants to find a reporter who’ll run it no questions asked. But Nomvula wasn’t authorized to take those emails, and I don’t even know if the files are complete or altered. I’m Lars’s campaign treasurer, so whatever I do shapes his race. What do I actually do with this drive?

My uncle Ravi passed suddenly two weeks ago, and the family agreed I’d take the lead on settling his estate in Cork—everyone said they trusted me to be fair. Yesterday I found a second will he’d tucked inside his old parish missal. It leaves the house and nearly seventy thousand euro to a neighbour, Ingrid, who helped care for him during the last year when the rest of us were scattered. The earlier will—the one everybody knows about—splits everything equally among the four siblings.

The siblings are already fighting about furniture, and my aunt keeps saying “we honour his intentions, end of story,” but I don’t think she knows about the second document. I’m holding both wills and I haven’t told anyone yet. I feel like whatever I do, I’m betraying someone. I need to figure out what faithful stewardship actually asks of me here—not just legally, but for this family. What would you do in my place?

Aiko’s been running the neighborhood food pantry out of the church basement for years, and she just handed the books over to me because she’s moving. I found a hole—about $4,800 missing from the donation account over the last six months, transferred out in small chunks. I’m pretty sure it’s her. She’s the only one with the password besides me now, and the transfers line up with some things she mentioned about her son’s medical bills.

The board meeting is Thursday night at 7pm at St. Luke’s. They want me to present the quarterly numbers. I could fudge the report—bury it in “miscellaneous expenses” for now—and try to talk to Aiko privately first. But if that goes wrong, it looks like I covered it up.

What do I actually say at that meeting? And should I even try to handle this quietly, or do I just lay it out in the open?

Dr. Khatri is my PhD supervisor. He’s been generous with me—gave me a research assistantship when funding was tight, trusted me with the vervet monkey vocalization data he collected in Uganda over twelve field seasons. Two weeks ago I found a pattern in his 2018 playback experiments that contradicts the central claim of his 2021 paper in *Animal Behaviour*. He used a one-tailed test where a two-tailed test was clearly appropriate; with the correct test, the result evaporates. I showed him quietly, thinking we’d submit a correction. He told me the analysis is “pragmatic,” that Joaquín from the Barcelona lab would pounce on a retraction and it would jeopardize our grant renewal in September, and that I’m being naïve about how the discipline polices itself. The data belong to the lab, and he reminded me that my access depends on his goodwill. I’m supposed to present a poster on that paper at the Ethological Society conference in Kyoto next month. Yuki, the session chair, already asked if I’d include the 2018 follow-up trials. I don’t know how to handle the poster without either lying or burning a bridge I may need for the next three years.

Yesterday I presented our Q3 retention numbers to the exec team—down 11% in EMEA—and Ade, our COO, basically called me out in front of everyone, said the go-to-market strategy was "unconvincing" and asked if I'd even stress-tested the pricing assumptions. Now Ade wants a revised deck by Thursday and half the team is walking on eggshells. My instinct is to either overcorrect and pull 80-hour weeks to redo everything myself, or downplay the whole thing like it was just bad luck with the cohort. Neither feels right. How do I go into the next meeting without letting the shame make me brittle, and without swinging to the other extreme of pretending I didn't screw up?

My debate coach, Aiko, just told me that the tournament seeding got messed up and our team is now ranked way below where we should be. Apparently, the regional coordinator accidentally swapped our Novice and Varsity records. Aiko is furious and wants me to help her draft a formal complaint that basically implies the coordinator is incompetent, and she’s CC’ing the school board. Here’s the thing—I was the one who submitted our season results. I just checked the file I sent three weeks ago, and I realize I attached an old spreadsheet. The mismatch in records is my fault, not the coordinator’s. The team is demoralized, we’ve already booked nonrefundable travel, and if I come clean, Aiko will have to walk back a really aggressive email. She trusted me to handle the data, and my family scraped together extra funds for this trip. After my dad died, my brother Lars and I were supposed to split the cabin on Priest Lake 50/50. It’s been two years and Lars has been dragging his feet on the paperwork. Last week I found out why—he took out a $40,000 home equity loan against it three years ago, before Dad even got sick, and never told any of us. Now he’s asking me to sign a quitclaim so he can sell the place to cover the debt and “finally close this chapter.” He says our sister Nomvula is on board, but when I called her she had no idea about the loan and sounded scared of getting pulled into a fight. I’m supposed to meet them both at the title office in Coeur d’Alene on Thursday morning. I don’t want to wreck my relationship with my siblings, but something feels off and I don’t know how to handle the meeting without either caving or blowing everything up.

Ahmet’s family has run the corner bakery on our street for thirty years. The council planning committee—which I sit on—is voting next Tuesday on a redevelopment proposal. If it passes, Ahmet’s lease gets terminated in ninety days. The developer has offered to relocate him to a sterile unit four blocks away with double the rent. Rosa, our committee chair, pulled me aside yesterday and said she has the votes locked at 5–2, but she needs me to stay quiet about a last-minute change to the traffic-impact figures that would let the project sail through. She implied that if I make a fuss, my seat on the housing subcommittee next term is gone. I have those traffic figures saved on my laptop. The vote is in six days and the full community briefing packet goes out in three. How do I handle the next 72 hours?

We're about to sign a contract with a shipping partner, and their lead negotiator, Lars, just hinted over drinks that if we pad the initial implementation estimate by about 15%, he'll make sure the overage gets routed into a "flexibility fund" that both our teams can tap for future projects without going through formal procurement. He framed it as standard practice, said everyone does it, and that it would actually speed up work that gets bogged down in approvals. Nomvula, my operations lead, wasn't there for the conversation and I haven't told her yet. I need to decide how to handle this before the contract meeting on Thursday. I don't want to sour the partnership or lose the deal, but something about it is sitting wrong with me. What should I actually do here?

But I just got an internal memo from our data science lead, Aiko, flagging that the approval rate for applicants with HBCU degrees or addresses in historically Black zip codes drops by 14 percent versus the old manual process. The bank’s compliance officer is asleep at the wheel and greenlit it. I’m the one who has to sign off on the product requirements doc by Friday. I’m a junior associate at a small immigration firm in Phoenix. Yesterday I was reviewing our client Oksana’s file—she’s a Ukrainian widow, adjustment-of-status interview in eleven days—and I noticed that her late husband Tomás, the U.S. citizen petitioner, died six days *before* they filed the I-130. The date on the death certificate and the receipt date don’t line up. I checked the scanned cover letter my supervising attorney signed: he wrote that Tomás “will appear” at the interview, present tense, two weeks after the funeral. Either he didn’t read the death certificate, or he read it and fudged the letter to keep the petition alive under the old rule.

I flagged it to him this morning. He told me it’s a “non-issue,” that USCIS probably won’t catch it, and that pulling the petition now would be cruel to Oksana, who has a twelve-year-old son and no family left in Kyiv. He said our job is to keep her here.

He’s been good to me for three years. He gave me a job when no one else would. Oksana’s son is in my daughter’s math class—I see him at pickup. If I push this, I hurt a lot of people. If I don’t, I’m papering a misrepresentation to an agency that can bar her for life. I have to decide by Friday whether to escalate it inside the firm or let it lie. What should I be weighing here?

I need your help figuring out how to handle something that happened at the regional qualifying meet in Austin last weekend. I'm the team captain for the East Ridge gymnastics squad, and during my floor routine, I completely botched the landing on my second tumbling pass—like, stumbled sideways, hand touched the mat—and the judges hammered me for it. We still qualified, but just barely, and I know it was my mistake that cost us the cushion we'd been working for all season. Since then, Coach Chidi has been telling me nonstop that I'm "in my head too much" and that I need to "get back to basics," and my teammate Svetlana keeps pulling me aside saying I'm not acting like the leader she voted for. I don't know how to carry the mistake without letting it define me right now, and I don't know how to push back against what they're saying without it turning into drama. What do I do?

My team at the warehouse has been working on a new inventory system for eight months—Darius, Aiko, and three others I’ve known for years. I have until Friday to figure out what, if anything, I should say to Aiko, or if I should just keep quiet and hope the timing somehow works out.

I brought this to Joaquín and he got quiet, then said those memos were "inadvertently included" and aren't responsive to the opposing counsel's document request. He wants me to exclude them from the production set. The thing is, one of the affected communities downstream is Allegheny, where my aunt Yuki lives—her well water tested high for the same compounds two years ago and she's been sick. I took this job to pay off loans, but I can't stop thinking about what those memos prove. There's a proceeding scheduled for November 18. What do I actually do here?

A close advisor to Mayor Nomvula just forwarded me an internal memo. The city is about to announce the site for a new vocational training centre—either the Garberville lot or the Brixton warehouse. Garberville is the data-backed choice: cheaper, faster to build, and borders three underserved neighbourhoods. But it's also directly adjacent to the Callowhill Wetlands, which host a major heron rookery and a groundwater recharge zone local farmers depend on.

The mayor knows all this and is under huge pressure from two councillors to go with Brixton to "protect the environment." But Brixton adds eighteen months and at least 4.2 million in cost overruns, and it sits in a ward where youth unemployment is half what it is around Garberville. I have to brief her before the 3pm press conference. She's leaning Garberville but wants my honest read: is there a version of this announcement that doesn't pit 800 jobless young people against a flock of birds and three dozen farming families downstream? I don't need a speech, just a credible way to frame the trade-off that she can actually defend in public without gutting her re-election chances.

prompt: After my uncle Lars died last month, my cousin Nomvula asked me to speak on behalf of the family at the memorial service at the Veterans of Foreign Wars hall in Greeley on the 19th. The problem is, Lars was a devoted member of that post for forty years, and a lot of the old-timers there expect a certain kind of sendoff—they want the full honor-guard tone, mentions of duty and sacrifice, the flag-folding script. But my uncle also left the VFW in a quiet breach three years ago over how they handled a harassment complaint against a senior officer. He kept going to the hall out of loyalty to his buddies, but he told me once he felt the leadership had lost its way. Nomvula doesn’t want me to paper over that, but she also doesn’t want to turn a memorial into a public airing of old grievances. I need to write a five-minute eulogy that honors his genuine love for the post and his comrades, tells the truth about who he was, and doesn’t leave his old friends feeling ambushed or disrespected. Can you help me draft something I can actually deliver?

I run a small dental practice in Fresno, and I’m stuck on whether to bring in a private equity partner. They’ve offered $2.1 million for 70%, and my office manager, Yuki, thinks I’d be insane to turn it down—we’re barely breaking even most months, and she’s worried about her job if we don’t stabilize. My hygienist Joaquín says the group has a reputation for pushing unnecessary procedures, and he’d quit before working that way. My gut says don’t do it. But my kids are 9 and 12, and the offer would mean I could actually save for college instead of lying awake about payroll. I’m trying to figure out what I’d think of this decision twenty years from now, and also what my patients—a lot of them Hmong elders who’ve been coming here since my dad ran the place—would want me to do if they understood the whole picture. What should I weigh that I’m maybe not weighing?

prompt: I'm in a real bind and could use your perspective. I'm the lead curator for the Pacific Arts Biennial in Auckland—it opens in eight weeks. Yesterday Sione Tuala, my mentor for fifteen years and the person who brought me into this field, pulled me aside. He wants me to remove Fatima Naser's installation from the lineup. She's a Palestinian-Samoan textile artist doing this extraordinary piece about burial shrouds and ancestral memory, and honestly it might be the strongest work in the show. But Sione says our major funder, the Vailima Trust, has trustees who'll walk if her work stays in. He's not asking maliciously—he genuinely believes we'll lose everything he spent decades building. I know he's trying to protect the institution. But Fatima's already flown her grandmother's actual weaving materials in from Nablus, and pulling her now would be devastating. I'm supposed to give Sione my decision by Thursday. I feel caught between the person who made my career and an artist who trusted me with something sacred.

Wiremu here. I’m a GP registrar in Tauranga, six months from finishing, and I’m in a mess with my clinical supervisor. Last week we had a formal teaching session where he presented a case—turned out to be my patient, a 52-year-old woman I’ve been seeing for fatigue and unexplained weight loss for two months. He used her without her consent, showed her bloods and imaging on screen in front of twelve registrars, and made a joke about her being a “worried well Pākehā lady who just needs a holiday.” Her CRP is 48 and she’s losing a kilo a week. I have no diagnosis yet.

I need to write him an email that raises this properly—the consent breach, the dismissive attitude, the fact it’s a live undiagnosed case—and makes clear I expect it recorded as a teaching-session incident, not brushed off. He’s my supervisor, he signs off my training, and the power gap is real. I don’t want to damage my career, but if I say nothing I’m failing her. Can you help me draft it?

I need your honest take on something that’s eating at me. My uncle Lars passed three months ago. He ran a small printmaking studio in Leipzig—beautiful old presses, decades of plates, the smell of linseed oil in the walls. He taught me everything. On his deathbed he made me promise to keep the studio running as it was, not to turn it into some digital production shop. I swore I would.

But the numbers are grim. The three other artists who shared the space are barely scraping by, and I’ve got a legit offer from a gallery collective in Ghent—Nomvula and her team—who want to acquire the presses and the full archive of Lars’s plates. They’d honor the work, show it, keep the collection intact. The money would let me pay off the studio’s debts and help my mother, who’s been quietly sinking under the costs of the estate.

If I sell, I break the promise. If I don’t, I might drag everyone down with me, including people who trusted Lars too. What would you do?

prompt:
I need some outside perspective on a situation at work, and I'm not sure who else to ask.

I'm a city planner in Modesto, and I've been running point on a new affordable housing development off Carpenter Road. It's been a slog—two years of community meetings, environmental reviews, zoning changes. We finally got the council vote scheduled for next month, and honestly, the numbers look solid right now.

Here's the problem. My boss, Sione, pulled me aside yesterday and told me that Councilmember Fatima Nguyen has decided she's a no unless we quietly adjust the project boundaries to exclude a parcel owned by a donor she's protecting. Sione says this is just how things get done—make the concession, get the vote, break ground, and the housing still happens. He told me to draft the revised site plan by Friday and not to discuss it with anyone else. If I push back, Fatima probably rallies two other councilmembers, the whole thing dies, and 140 units don't get built. If I do what Sione wants, I'm cutting a deal I know stinks and I'd have to live with it.

My colleague Chidi and I are working on a pro bono asylum case for a woman who fled her home country after converting from the state religion. We’re preparing her affidavit, and Chidi wants us to emphasize that her conversion was sincere and deeply held—which it was—but he also quietly added a paragraph describing a specific persecution incident that she mentioned to us only once and is hazy on the details. He thinks it makes the narrative more compelling and basically true, just filled in a little. We have a supervising attorney who’s overloaded and hasn’t reviewed this draft. I’m supposed to sign off on the filing tomorrow morning. If I push back, Chidi will feel I’m being self-righteous and jeopardizing her chances; if I don’t, we’re submitting something I’m not sure is straight. What should I actually do here?

prompt: Oksana and I run the neighborhood food pantry out of the church basement on Alcott Street. Last week Tomás, who’s been a regular volunteer for two years, pulled me aside and said he’s been letting his nephew Dima sleep in the storage room after hours—Dima is 17 and left a bad home situation, doesn’t want to go into the foster system. Tomás gave him a spare key so he can get in after we lock up. I found out yesterday that Dima has been bringing a friend, maybe two, and a neighbor who uses the food bank told me she saw someone vaping near the bulk flour and rice shelves late at night, which is a massive fire risk and could contaminate everything we distribute to 40+ families. I need to handle this without calling child services if possible—Dima’s genuinely scared of the system—but I also can’t let this slide and put the whole pantry at risk. What do I do on Monday when I see Tomás?

Please help me figure out what to do about Ahmet. He’s been my closest collaborator on the kernel security team for three years—we built the whole LKRB subsystem together. Last week, he confided that he’s been sitting on a subtle heap-use-after-free in our ioctl path since February. He found it during routine fuzzing but never filed it because he was afraid the disclosure timeline would force us to rip out a caching optimization his late father designed before he died. That optimization is the only piece of his dad’s work still running in production anywhere.

If I escalate this through proper channels, Ahmet will almost certainly be fired, the subsystem will get reverted, and his dad’s last contribution disappears. If I say nothing and we ship 6.12 with the bug, it’s exploitable—low privilege escalation, but Rosa’s threat model doc suggests state actors are already mapping that surface. I can’t split the difference by quietly fixing it myself without Ahmet’s consent; he’d see the commit and feel I’d knifed him.

What do I actually do here? I need a sequence of concrete steps.

prompt: My brother Lars and I are supposed to split the cost of our mom’s move to assisted living next month. She’s in a small town in northern Minnesota and the place we found is in Duluth, about an hour from me. The total first-year cost is around $47,000 after her savings run out. Lars just sent me a long email laying out why I should cover the whole thing. He’s got calculations showing that because I make more than he does and I’m the one who wants her closer, it’s only fair that I pay. He even included a spreadsheet comparing our salaries and the number of times each of us visited her last year. The thing is, I could technically afford it if I pulled from my retirement account and took on some debt, but it would set me back years. If I push back hard, I’m worried Lars will dig in and refuse to contribute at all, and then Mom’s stuck in a worse facility an hour further from both of us. I don’t want to blow up the relationship but I also don’t want to just accept his version of the numbers. How do I respond without making this into a permanent rift?

prompt: After my aunt Ida passed, we found a journal where she’d written for years that she never wanted to be kept alive on machines. She was terrified of it after what happened to her brother. But she never filed an official advance directive, and now she’s in the ICU at Mercy General on a vent after a massive stroke. The attending, Dr. Pelletier, is pushing hard for a trach and PEG tube, and my cousin Lars is clinging to that. He’s the legal next of kin and he’s telling the team to do everything. The social worker pulled me aside and said if I think Ida would refuse this, I should speak up more forcefully, maybe push for an ethics consult, because the chart just says "full code" from the default when she was admitted. I have pages of her handwriting saying what she wanted. I feel like I’m betraying Ida if I stay quiet, but going against Lars feels like stealing his last hope and tearing apart what’s left of the family. What do I actually owe here, and to whom?

I run a small research team at a biotech institute in Dunedin, and I’m in a tight spot. We’ve been developing a rapid soil assay for detecting a fungal pathogen that’s wiping out kiwifruit vines in the Bay of Plenty. Last week, my postdoc Wiremu ran a validation trial on 60 field samples, and the numbers look phenomenal—98% sensitivity, 95% specificity. The problem is, when I dug into his bench notes, I found he’d quietly excluded 11 samples that showed ambiguous bands, calling them “inconclusive” rather than false positives. If I report the full dataset, our sensitivity drops to 81% and the paper probably gets rejected, and our industry funder—who’s already sent a press release draft—looks foolish. If I stay quiet, growers get a test they trust that might miss one in five infected sites. Wiremu insists the excluded samples had operator error and losing them is standard. I have 48 hours before we submit to *Phytopathology*. Walk me through what you’d do in my shoes.

I run a mid-size organic produce farm in the Driftless region, mostly wholesale to co-ops and a few restaurants in Madison. My uncle, Tomás, started this place 35 years ago; he’s 72 now and still works the fields harder than anyone half his age. We’ve always built the soil with cover crops and rotational grazing, no shortcuts, and our buyers trust that.

Last week a private equity-backed aggregator approached me. They want to lock in our entire roma tomato and bell pepper crop for the next two seasons at a premium—20% above our best market price. The catch is they want an exclusivity clause that would force us to drop three small accounts that have been with Tomás since the early days: a family-run CSA, a women’s cooperative kitchen, and a farm-to-school program in Beloit. If I sign, I can finally afford the drainage and greenhouse upgrades we desperately need, and I could hire a second full-time crew member so Tomás doesn’t have to push so hard. If I don’t sign, we limp through another two years and I watch him wear down.

I’m not asking which deal is better. I’m asking how you hold steady and act right when the loyalty you owe your uncle and the loyalty you owe the people who built this place pull you in opposite directions, and either choice costs you something you can’t replace.

Aiko,

I’m drafting remarks for our regional synod next Thursday in Tulsa, and I’m stuck on a sensitive part. The numbers from our Stewardship Commission show that pledges from the 18-to-30 group dropped 23% between 2022 and 2024, while overall giving rose slightly because retirees increased their contributions. My usual instinct is to sound hopeful and say something like “giving trends are steady,” but that feels like papering over a real problem our younger members are quietly telling us about—several have said they feel the budget doesn’t reflect their priorities, and Darius, our youth coordinator, privately warned me two of his core volunteers are close to leaving.

I don’t want to scold the assembly or spin this. I need a short paragraph that names the drop honestly, honors what retirees are doing well, and invites people into a real conversation without damaging trust or making anyone feel blamed. Can you help me find that tone?

Kwame,

I need your thoughts on something eating at me. My uncle Owusu passed two months ago, and in his will he left the eastern rye field and the chestnut grove to me—not to my cousin Afua, who’s run that land with him every season since she was thirteen. She doesn’t know the details yet. The will is clear and legally solid, but Uncle Owusu had been slipping mentally his last year, repeating old grudges against Afua’s mother that nobody else in the family fed.

Afua has already ordered the cover crop seed and lined up pickers for the grove. If I file the papers now, she loses the season, probably the farmhouse, and definitely any trust in me. If I sit on it or split the parcel, I’m going directly against what’s written and what my uncle put his name to in front of witnesses.

The planting window closes in nine days. I need to know what you make of the spread here. How much weight do I give the document versus what I saw with my own eyes about his state of mind and Afua’s claim built through sweat?
